core: minimum-access principle: users and programs get only the access their jobs require
why it matters: limits the damage a compromised account can do
where it applies: user accounts, administrator rights, programs and services, cloud permissions
administrator versus standard accounts (the everyday pattern)
privilege creep: access that accumulates and is never removed
regular access reviews: reviewing and removing access
honest framing: least privilege reduces risk but does not eliminate it
supporting: horizontal and vertical application of least privilege
elevation: temporarily using administrator rights for a specific task
outOfScope: how authorization systems decide and enforce permissions (own topic: authorization)
zero-trust architecture and its other principles (own topic: zero-trust-basics)

claims.claim: Least privilege is the principle that a security architecture is designed so that each entity is granted the minimum system resources and authorizations that the entity needs to perform its function.
In practical terms, least privilege means assigning users only the minimum privileges necessary to complete their job.
Least privilege access means users and workloads get only the access they need, for the shortest time required.
The core benefit of least privilege is containment: an attacker who takes over an account inherits only the access that account held, so limited rights mean limited damage.
Least privilege must be applied both horizontally (across people at the same level of an organization) and vertically (according to responsibility).
In cloud environments, least privilege means granting only the permissions required to perform a task and working to reduce broad grants toward least-privilege permissions over time.
Running as a standard user helps maximize security; even administrator accounts run everyday tasks in a standard-user security context unless a specific task is elevated with approval.
Access tends to accumulate because it is easier to grant users additional permissions than to take away ones they previously enjoyed, which is why periodic access reviews are needed.

positions: Some users and administrators prefer broad standing access because it avoids repeated approvals and makes work faster.
Security guidance holds that broad access enlarges the damage any single compromise can do, so access should be limited to what a job needs.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents least privilege as the security-better default and shows the practical balance: standard accounts for daily work, elevation for specific tasks, and periodic reviews so limits do not drift. Convenience is treated as a reason access creeps, not as a reason to abandon the principle.

sourceRecords.title: Zero Trust overview
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl 2026-08-21. Supports the 'Use least privilege access' principle: 'User and workloads get only the access they need, for the shortest time required,' and the assume-breach framing that controls focus on limiting breach impact. Zero-trust architecture itself is out of scope for this lesson; only the least-privilege principle is cited.

sourceRecords.title: How User Account Control works
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl 2026-08-21. Supports: running as a standard user helps maximize security; by default both standard and administrator users access resources and run apps in the security context of a standard user; a standard user performing an administrative task receives a credential prompt, while an administrator in Admin Approval Mode receives a consent prompt. Basis for the administrator-versus-standard account section.

sourceRecords.title: IAM Best Practices (AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl 2026-08-21. Supports 'Apply least-privilege permissions': when setting permissions with IAM policies, grant only the permissions required to perform a task; teams may start broad and work toward least-privilege permissions as the use case matures. Cited for the cloud-permissions application of least privilege.
